title: A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research
extended_summary:
This paper reviews the field of self-regulated learning (SRL) by analyzing and comparing six major SRL models: Zimmerman, Boekaerts, Winne and Hadwin, Pintrich, Efklides, and Hadwin, Järvelä, and Miller. The central question is how these models conceptualize the cognitive, metacognitive, motivational, emotional, and social processes involved in students regulating their own learning, and what implications these models have for research and educational practice. The review also considers existing meta-analytic evidence on SRL and proposes future directions for the field.

Rather than testing a single intervention, the paper synthesizes theoretical and empirical literature associated with each model. For each model, the author discusses its historical development, core components and phases, empirical support, and associated measurement instruments. The paper also compares models on key dimensions such as phases and subprocesses, treatment of cognition, motivation, and emotion, top-down versus bottom-up processing, automaticity, and contextual influences. In this sense, the paper is a broad conceptual and literature review of SRL frameworks rather than an intervention study.

The populations represented in the reviewed evidence span multiple educational levels, including high school students, college/undergraduate students, and broader K-12 contexts depending on the studies cited under each model. The article is written for educational psychology researchers and practitioners, including teachers, and extracts implications for helping students become more strategic and successful learners. Although the author is based in Spain, the paper reviews international literature rather than reporting a single country-based empirical sample.

The main conclusion is that SRL models together form an integrative and coherent framework for understanding and improving learning. The review argues that these models have substantial empirical support, but also that their effects and relevance may differ by developmental stage and educational level. The author concludes that researchers and teachers should apply SRL models more deliberately in ways tailored to students' age and context, and identifies four future lines of research to advance the field.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed narrative review with explicit inclusion criteria, but it is not a meta-analysis and does not provide systematic causal synthesis focused on a defined intervention/outcome comparison. It offers useful theoretical and descriptive evidence but limited direct causal evidence for K-12 writing interventions.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests broadly positive but heterogeneous effects of SRL-related approaches, yet it reports no pooled impact estimate and is not focused on a specific high-school writing intervention or comparator condition. Impact is therefore unclear for the target use case of improving grades 9-12 writing quality.

finding.finding_summary: This is a narrative review of self-regulated learning (SRL) models rather than a single intervention study. It synthesizes prior empirical and meta-analytic evidence suggesting that SRL-related supports are generally associated with improvements in motivation, self-efficacy, emotion regulation, and strategic learning, but effects vary by developmental stage, educational level, and model features; no pooled effect size is reported in this review itself.
finding.measure: Self-regulated learning, motivation, self-efficacy, emotion regulation, and related self-report or observational measures summarized from prior studies

finding.finding_summary: The review concludes that SRL models provide an integrative framework for teaching students to become more strategic and successful learners, with prior cited studies showing gains in metacognitive strategy use, monitoring, planning, and collaborative/shared regulation of learning. However, this paper does not present new experimental estimates, and no unified effect size or sample is reported because findings are aggregated narratively across many prior studies.
finding.measure: Metacognition, planning, monitoring, strategic learning behaviors, shared regulation/collaboration, and related SRL processes
